rationale: A wins because it keeps the angle set bolted to the actual facts and shows exactly where each pitch breaks: "Without the pricing model, this angle is an assertion, not a story — get it first." B has usable bones, but it overreaches with "becoming a mass-market consumer bank," which the update does not support. A's "Mercury opens consumer accounts to customers it doesn't hold deposits for" is a sharper banking-structure story than B's fuzzier SVB-to-consumer framing.
gaps_in_A: "Mercury opens consumer accounts to customers it doesn't hold deposits for" is a little too clever. Mercury does not hold deposits directly, but the customer relationship is still Mercury-facing; the headline risks overstating the structure.

"A profitable fintech is walking into the market that broke the unprofitable ones" leans on a broad neobank thesis not supplied in the update. A saves itself by demanding proof, but the headline carries more certainty than the facts do.

"Mercury picks a fight with neobanks and big banks at the same time" only works if Mercury Personal has concrete features, rates, or terms worth comparing. A admits the gap, but the angle is thin until that proof exists.
gaps_in_B: "mass-market consumer bank" is overclaimed. The update says invite-only personal checking and savings with a waitlist, partner-bank services, and no Mercury bank charter.
"the market it spent years defining itself against" invents positioning. The facts say Mercury served startups, not that it publicly defined itself against consumers.
"well-capitalized" is not in the update. Profitability and 200,000 business customers do not prove capitalization.
"When a business-only fintech decides it's ready to be a full-service bank" overstates the product. Checking and savings through partner banks is not enough to call Mercury full-service or a bank.
